name: Northwest Semitic
defining_innovation: Word-initial *w became y: Hebrew yeled 'child' beside Arabic walad, which keeps the old w.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
Northwest Semitic is the Semitic of the Levant and Syria in the Bronze and Iron Ages. Its earliest traces are the names of **Amorites**, West Semitic newcomers who appear in Mesopotamian records around 2000 BCE and who founded dynasties at Mari and Babylon. Hammurabi's name is Amorite. A clear shared change is at the start of words, where `*w` became *y*: Hebrew *yeled* 'child' corresponds to Arabic *walad*.

Its two great branches are **Canaanite** (Hebrew, Phoenician, Moabite) and **Aramaic**. **Ugaritic**, the language of the city of Ugarit on the Syrian coast, is also Northwest Semitic, but whether it is a form of Canaanite or a separate branch is disputed.

chapters.title: Ugarit
chapters.body: Ugarit's scribes of the 14th–13th centuries BCE wrote their language in a unique alphabet of 30 wedge-shaped signs, an alphabet pressed into clay in cuneiform style. Its myths of the storm god Baal and the ruler god El illuminate Canaanite religion and the background of the Hebrew Bible. The city was destroyed around 1185 BCE in the upheavals at the end of the Bronze Age, and the language disappeared with it.

speakers.note: Hebrew accounts for about 5 million first-language speakers; the Neo-Aramaic languages are all endangered.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.
Moseley, Christopher, ed. 2010. Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger, 3rd ed. Paris: UNESCO Publishing.

turning_points.title: Amorites in Mesopotamia
turning_points.description: Amorite names fill Mesopotamian records as West Semitic groups establish dynasties at Mari and Babylon. The language is known only from names. Its precise relationship to later Northwest Semitic is debated.

sources.citation: Huehnergard, John & Aaron D. Rubin. 2011. Phyla and waves: Models of classification of the Semitic languages. In The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook, ed. Stefan Weninger. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

turning_points.title: Initial *w becomes y
turning_points.description: At the start of a word, `*w` becomes *y*: Hebrew *yeled* 'child' against Arabic *walad*. Inside words the old *w* often survives, so the change shows up as alternations within verb families.

sources.citation: Sáenz-Badillos, Angel. 1993. A History of the Hebrew Language. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: The Ugaritic alphabet
turning_points.description: Ugarit writes its language in a 30-sign alphabet in cuneiform style, with its own letter order. Abecedaries found at the site show that this order is ancestral to the order of the later Semitic and Greek alphabets.

sources.citation: Hetzron, Robert, ed. 1997. The Semitic Languages. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Canaanite and Aramaic diverge
turning_points.description: In the Iron Age, the Canaanite dialects of the coast and southern Levant and the Aramaic of inland Syria develop into separate language groups, each soon with its own writing tradition.

sources.citation: Gzella, Holger. 2015. A Cultural History of Aramaic. Leiden: Brill.
